label: RCA Victor
rationale: Mingus's own favourite among his records — he called it 'the best thing I've ever done' — and the fullest early statement of his long-form compositional method: a five-part Tijuana suite cut over two sessions, July 18 and August 6, 1957, at RCA Victor's Studio A in New York, with Clarence Shaw, Jimmy Knepper, Shafi Hadi, Bill Triglia and Dannie Richmond, plus percussionist Frankie Dunlop and castanet/vocal contributions from Ysabel Morel and Lonne Elder III [S1,S2,S3,S4] (obs). Held back five years by a legal dispute with RCA and finally issued in June 1962, it arrived alongside Oh Yeah as the record that re-established Mingus as a major composer [S1,S5] (obs). Consensus/reception: Wikipedia's review box records AllMusic 5/5, The Penguin Guide to Jazz 3.5/5 (2000 expanded edition), The Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 5/5 and Tom Hull 'A'; DownBeat called it 'the 1957 masterpiece on which Mingus asserts full control over his longform chops' [S1] (obs). Session gravity is high — the date pulls together the band Mingus was working with in the late 1950s, overlapping with the ensemble that would make Mingus Ah Um two years later [S1,S3] (inf). It still plays: 'Ysabel's Table Dance' and 'Los Mariachis' remain among the most vivid programmatic writing in jazz, and the album is the clearest single answer to the question of what Mingus's notation was for [S1,S4] (inf).

personnel_record.notes: Two sessions, both at RCA Victor's Studio A, New York City: July 18 and August 6, 1957. Producer Bob Rolontz and engineer Bob Simpson are named by the reissue liner notes [S4] and the Discogs credit list [S3]; AllMusic and Wikipedia print no engineer [S1,S2]. Per-track session split is taken from the Discogs back-cover key ('July 18 (A1, A2, B2) and August 6, 1957 (B1, B3)') against that pressing's side layout (A1 Dizzy Moods, A2 Ysabel's Table Dance; B1 Tijuana Gift Shop, B2 Los Mariachis, B3 Flamingo), giving July 18 = Dizzy Moods, Ysabel's Table Dance, Los Mariachis and August 6 = Tijuana Gift Shop, Flamingo; no independent source spells this mapping out per track, so it is recorded at side-level confidence [S3]. Recorded for RCA's subsidiary Vik label per the 1962 New York Times review quoted by Microgroove [S5] — label of record is RCA Victor. Year field is the 1957 recording year (the release date is June/August 1962, all sources) to match the album's placement in jazz discographies and its place in Mingus's 1957 output. The 1986 New Tijuana Moods and later CD expansions add alternate takes and 'A Colloquial Dream (Scenes in the City)'; these are reissue-only and excluded above. Durations are the original LP timings [S3]. All nine personnel are credited on all five issued tracks by the sources; no source distinguishes per-track personnel, so track_assignments_complete is false. Mingus wrote all five pieces except 'Flamingo' (Ted Grouya/Edmund Anderson) and 'Dizzy Moods', a reworking of Gillespie's 'Woody 'n You' credited to Mingus and Gillespie [S3].

ballot.case_for: The album is a defining early statement of Mingus's long-form, programmatic writing, integrating castanets, vocals, and street-band color into pieces such as “Ysabel's Table Dance” and “Los Mariachis” (S1, S3, S4). Its critical standing is strong across AllMusic, the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide, Tom Hull, and DownBeat, while its late-1950s ensemble includes key Mingus collaborators Jimmy Knepper and Dannie Richmond (S1, S2, S3).
ballot.case_against: The album was recorded in 1957 but withheld until 1962, so it could not shape the late-1950s scene in real time as its lineage might otherwise suggest (S1, S5). The Penguin Guide's 3.5/5 rating is positive but below its top tier, and if Mingus Ah Um is already represented, the council must judge whether Tijuana Moods' distinctive suite-like, programmatic dimension adds enough beyond that landmark to justify another Mingus album (S1).
ballot.disagreement: One reference judged the album contested, emphasizing the genuine overlap question with Mingus Ah Um and the Penguin rating; the other judged it consensus_core, treating its compositional importance and broad critical praise as decisive. Both rated it strong rather than must_have and noted that the delayed release muted its contemporary influence.
ballot.recommendation: John should give Tijuana Moods strong consideration as a distinct Mingus statement, weighing its programmatic suite writing against the possibility that Mingus Ah Um already covers the essential ground.
